definition: Coagulate means to thicken and set into a semi-solid mass.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word coagulate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know coagulate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Left open overnight, the pot of hide glue had coagulated into a rubbery mass no amount of stirring could loosen.
To thicken is the first, mildest step on this scale — a sauce thickens and still pours — while to coagulate is to cross the line into a semi-solid mass that holds its shape.
Solidify goes past coagulate — coagulated blood is a soft, quivering mass; solidified wax is hard all the way through.

Clot is the word blood itself takes — blood clots at a cut, and surgeons watch for clots. Coagulate covers the same setting in any liquid at all: egg white, latex, hide glue. Every clot has set this way, but a pot of glue coagulates and no one calls it a clot.

Set is the kitchen's gentle word for the same change — custard sets, jelly sets, cement sets — and it sounds friendly at the table. Coagulate is the laboratory's and the clinic's term, precise about the mechanism and often carrying an unappetizing edge the cook would rather avoid.

Coagulate is the exact word because it means to thicken and set into a semi-solid mass.
It names a one-way change of state, liquid crossing over into something that holds its shape.
Cooling is not required and neither is spoiling; what matters is the setting, the moment the liquid stops pouring and starts sitting.

People and plans do not coagulate: when a crowd or a committee draws together, the word is coalesce, a different Latin verb about growing, not driving.

Combat medics carry gauze that is anything but ordinary.
Each roll is treated with a powdered mineral that makes blood coagulate within seconds of touching a wound, instead of the several minutes an untreated cut can take.
The difference sounds small until you learn that uncontrolled bleeding is the leading preventable cause of death in the field.
Researchers borrowed the idea from the body itself, which stacks sticky proteins at a cut until the flow halts and a soft seal forms.
The treated gauze simply crowds more of those proteins into one place at once, hurrying a process the bloodstream already knows how to run.
